cenas.titulo: 2008: why Bitcoin was born
cenas.fala: In October 2008, a short document appeared that changed the conversation about money. Let's look at the context.

cenas.titulo: In 2008, the financial world was in crisis.
itens: Governments and central banks rushed to rescue institutions.

cenas.fala: In 2008, the financial world was in crisis. Large banks had lent money to people who couldn't repay it, and the problem spread through the whole system. Governments and central banks rushed to rescue institutions. Many people lost their home, their job or their savings. It was in this context that many people started asking whether the traditional financial system was the only possible path.

cenas.fala: On 31 October 2008, a document with that title appeared on the internet. It was signed by a person using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. To this day, nobody knows for sure who that person is, or whether it's a group. That's the first strange thing, and it's worth keeping in mind, because it forces us to judge the idea and not the person.

cenas.fala: The central idea was simple to say and hard to do. Money that could be sent from one person to another without going through a bank, without an intermediary approving every transfer. Instead of relying on trust in an institution, it relied on a rule written in code, which the whole network checked. That's the difference to hold on to: trust in a person versus trust in a process.

cenas.titulo: The notebook nobody erases
cenas.fala: Imagine a notebook that the whole village has, and that nobody can tear up without everyone noticing.

cenas.titulo: Imagine a village where everyone has an account book.
itens: Only here there's one rule.
There isn't a single notebook kept by the head of the parish council.

cenas.fala: Imagine a village where everyone has an account book. Every time someone owes money to another person, a line is written: who paid, who to, how much, and the date. Only here there's one rule. There isn't a single notebook kept by the head of the parish council. Everyone has a copy, and the copies are updated together. That is, in very simple terms, a blockchain: a chain of blocks, where each block is a page with several lines.

cenas.titulo: Let's go step by step.
cenas.fala: Let's go step by step. First, the lines. A transaction says: this wallet sent so many units of this currency to that wallet. Second, the pages. A block bundles several transactions and closes when it's full, or when a certain amount of time has passed. Third, the link between pages. Each page has a kind of seal that results from the content of the page before it. Technically it's called a hash function, but think of it as a fingerprint of the content: if the content changes, the fingerprint changes. If someone alters an old line, the seal no longer matches, and all the following pages become invalid.

cenas.titulo: This is what makes the notebook hard to erase.
itens: It's not that changing anything is impossible.
And that majority has copies of the notebook.

cenas.fala: This is what makes the notebook hard to erase. It's not that changing anything is impossible. It's that changing it means redoing the whole path, and it has to be accepted by the majority of the network. And that majority has copies of the notebook. Anyone trying to tamper with an old page has to convince the whole village that the story is different. In practice, that doesn't happen.

cenas.fala: But then, who writes the new page? This is where many people find things confusing, and I'll simplify it. There are two main methods. The first is called proof of work, or mining. Computers compete to solve a difficult mathematical problem. Whoever solves it first writes the next page and receives a reward. It uses a lot of energy, and it's the method Bitcoin uses. The second is called proof of stake. Instead of competing with calculation, participants lock up coins as collateral, and the system chooses who writes the page. If that person tries to cheat, they lose the collateral. This is the method the Ethereum network adopted in September 2022, in a transition called The Merge.

Once you understand this, the way you think about security changes, because you stop looking for where the coins are and start looking for where the keys are. cenas.titulo: DCA, the boring method that takes the guesswork out
cenas.fala: There is a way of investing that almost nobody wants to hear about, because it is boring. That is exactly why it takes the guesswork out of the equation.

cenas.titulo: DCA stands for regular buying, or dollar cost averaging.
itens: The idea is simple.
Instead of investing everything at once, you buy a fixed amount at regular intervals.
It can be one hundred euros a month, or twenty euros a week.
cenas.fala: DCA stands for regular buying, or dollar cost averaging. The idea is simple. Instead of investing everything at once, you buy a fixed amount at regular intervals. It can be one hundred euros a month, or twenty euros a week. You buy when the price is high and you buy when it is low, without trying to pick the right moment. The goal is not to hit the top or the bottom of the market. It is to stay disciplined for a long time, without relying on a hunch that makes you stop or speed up. This is the part that sounds unexciting, and it is also the part most people give up on. Think of it as the monthly savings you put aside, except that instead of leaving it sitting still, you put it into an asset.

In the first month it costs fifty euros, so you buy two units.
In the third month it goes back up to fifty, and you buy two more.

cenas.fala: Let's look at an illustrative example, with made-up, round prices, just to understand the mechanics. Imagine you buy one hundred euros a month, for three months, in a hypothetical asset. In the first month it costs fifty euros, so you buy two units. In the second month the price drops to twenty-five, and with the same one hundred euros you buy four units. In the third month it goes back up to fifty, and you buy two more. In total you have eight units and you have spent three hundred euros. Your average price per unit is thirty-seven euros and fifty cents. Notice that this figure is below the simple average of the three prices, because you bought more when it was cheap.

cenas.fala: Now the comparison. If you had invested the full three hundred euros in the first month, at fifty euros, you would have six units. At the end of the example, with the price back at fifty, the eight DCA units are worth four hundred euros, and the six lump-sum units are worth three hundred. But look at the middle of the path. After the second month, with the price at twenty-five, DCA has six units, worth one hundred and fifty euros on two hundred invested. The lump sum also has six units and is worth one hundred and fifty, but on three hundred invested. In percentage terms, the lump sum is down fifty percent and DCA is down twenty-five percent.

cenas.titulo: Not a guarantee of profit
cenas.fala: Now notice what this example does not say. It does not say that DCA is always better. If the price had risen in the first month and never come back down, the lump sum would have earned much more. DCA trades part of that opportunity for less stress and less risk of buying everything at the top. It is not a guarantee of profit, and an asset can fall for years without recovering. So the amount you use in each purchase has to be an amount you can afford to lose, without it affecting your income, your bills or your sleep.

cenas.titulo: Halving: the supply clock
cenas.fala: Roughly every four years, the creation of new bitcoins is cut in half. Do you know why, and do you know what that really means?

cenas.titulo: New bitcoins are created by miners, as a reward for validating blocks of transactions.
cenas.fala: New bitcoins are created by miners, as a reward for validating blocks of transactions. That reward is not fixed. It is set in the protocol itself: every 210,000 blocks, which takes about four years on average, the reward per block is cut in half. This is called the halving. When the network started, in 2009, the reward was fifty bitcoins per block. In 2012 it dropped to twenty-five. In 2016 it went to twelve point five, in 2020 to six point two five, and in 2024 to three point one two five. Each step cuts the new supply in half. Notice that the rule does not depend on any one person: it is written in the code and applies in the same way to everyone.

cenas.titulo: This is a fact about new supply, and that is what makes the topic interesting.
itens: Fewer new bitcoins per day means, in theory, less supply entering the market.
But theory and price are different things, and this is where many people get it wrong.
Supply is one piece of the puzzle.
cenas.fala: With this rule, the total supply converges towards the limit of twenty-one million bitcoins. Most of it has already been issued, and what remains comes out in smaller and smaller slices, almost unnoticed. This is a fact about new supply, and that is what makes the topic interesting. Fewer new bitcoins per day means, in theory, less supply entering the market. Miners also pay for energy and equipment, so the drop in reward has a big effect on their accounts. But theory and price are different things, and this is where many people get it wrong. Supply is one piece of the puzzle. Demand, context and the mood of all the participants are the other pieces.

cenas.fala: It is tempting to look at past halvings and conclude that the price always rises after each one. That conclusion is dangerous. There are too few cases to draw a rule from, the context changed a lot from one cycle to the next, and the market may have anticipated the event months earlier. Each halving is a fact about supply, not a date marked for a price rise. Use it as information to understand the market, never as a certainty about what will happen.

cenas.titulo: Cycles, volatility and dominance: reading without guessing
cenas.fala: The crypto market goes up and down with a force that frightens anyone who is not prepared. The question is not how to get it right. It is how to read it without guessing.

cenas.titulo: drops of more than 70% in different years
cenas.fala: Let's start with volatility, which is the size of price movements. In crypto it is very high. Bitcoin has fallen more than seventy percent from its peak, on more than one occasion, and many other coins have fallen even further. Before you buy, ask yourself an honest question: if my balance fell by half, could I carry on without selling in a panic? If the answer is no, your exposure is too big, whatever the videos say. This question is worth more than any forecast.

itens: Nobody knows exactly when the phase changes.

cenas.fala: Many people talk about cycles: a phase of accumulation, a strong rise, a euphoria in which everyone seems rich, then a long decline and a period of exhaustion. Cycles are a useful way of reading the past, because they help you recognise patterns of human behaviour. But they are not a calendar. In the euphoria it seems the whole world has got rich, and in the decline it seems it will never recover. Nobody knows exactly when the phase changes. There is a dangerous phrase you hear in every cycle: this time is different. Sometimes there are real changes, but the wish for it to be different is always the same old emotion. cenas.fala: Another indicator is bitcoin dominance, which is the percentage of the total market value that belongs to bitcoin. When dominance rises, money tends to concentrate in bitcoin, which is seen as the most established asset. When it falls, there can be more appetite for altcoins, which are riskier and more volatile coins. It is not a magic rule, and it can mislead you if you read it on its own. But it is a way of seeing where the money is going, and that is already useful information for your plan. Notice that dominance also rises when the market falls back, because smaller coins usually drop harder.

cenas.fala: Learn to separate news from noise. News is a verifiable fact: a law passed, a confirmed technical failure, a concrete change in supply or regulation. Before you react, ask: has this changed anything in the project, or has it only changed people's mood? If it is only mood, you usually do not need to act today. A good habit is to save the news in a list and review that list a week later. If nobody is talking about it any more, it was probably noise.

Smart DCA always buys too, but it lets you adjust the size of each purchase depending on whether the market is more expensive or cheaper than usual. Notice the word “always”. Smart DCA never stops buying because of an opinion. It only changes the size.

If you top up a little more on the days of decline and a little less on the days of euphoria, your average price tends to become more balanced. Tends to. I don't guarantee anything, and nobody can guarantee anything to you. But it is a line of reasoning you can understand and check with pencil and paper.

cenas.titulo: The four labels
cenas.fala: At MoreThanMoney this has a name: DCA Inteligente. Every day the system looks at the assets in the portfolios, crypto and ETFs, compares today's price with recent behaviour, and gives each one one of four labels. Forte Compra, which means strong buy, when there has been a sharp drop. Compra, which means buy, when there has been a relevant drop. Aguardar, which means wait, when everything is calm. And Não Reforçar, which means do not top up, when the price has risen a lot in a single day and it is best not to chase it.

cenas.titulo: The four labels
cenas.fala: Each label comes with a suggested size, always relative to your base amount. In crypto, for example, a daily drop of eight percent or more gives Forte Compra and suggests up to double the base. A drop of four percent or more gives Compra, and suggests one and a half times the base. For ETFs the thresholds are lower, because they move less. Remember: these are suggestions from a system, for education. The decision is yours.

cenas.texto: The ceiling matters more than the label.
cenas.fala: And now the rule that makes this safe. Your monthly ceiling does not change. If your plan is one hundred euros a month, it is one hundred euros a month, whether there is a Forte Compra or not. How does that work? With a reserve pot. In the weeks when the label says Aguardar or Não Reforçar, the part you don't spend goes into the pot. In the weeks of Forte Compra, the extra top-up comes out of the pot. If the pot is empty, you buy the base and that's it. You never go and get money from outside the plan.

cenas.fala: Before you set up anything, I want you to understand one thing. In a portfolio, the most important question is not which coin I buy. It is how much of my money goes into each piece, and why. This module is about that question. We are going to build the portfolio in layers, from the most stable to the riskiest, and each layer has its own role. If you have got this far, you already know what DCA is and you already have your plan, with a base amount, a fixed day and a ceiling. What is missing is giving shape to what you buy. It is usually made up of the best-known assets with the longest history, and that is where your DCA spends most of its time. The satellites are the smaller part: smaller, more volatile assets, each with its own thesis, which you must be able to explain in two sentences. The core weathers the storms. They are a way of making visible a decision that, without paper, stays hidden in a Thursday-night impulse. Once the decision is written down, it is much harder to take it badly on impulse. If the answer is “because it went up a lot last week”, that is not a thesis, it is a headline. Write the thesis before you buy, and review it once a month. If you can no longer explain why it is there, take it out of the satellites. Careful: DCA does not stop because of that. It is the plan that changes, in the notebook, calmly, and never in the middle of a drop. The new money then goes somewhere else in the plan.

itens: A very common trap is holding twelve assets with one-euro slices.
If you are thinking about more, wait.
cenas.fala: A very common trap is holding twelve assets with one-euro slices. It looks like diversification, but in practice it is a collection of decisions you do not understand. Anyone starting should have a core of one or two assets and, at most, two or three satellites. If you are thinking about more, wait. You can always add later, once you have the habit of writing the thesis and recording every purchase. Fewer assets, more thesis, and a DCA you actually follow, rather than a DCA lost on a screen full of coins.

cenas.fala: Let us look at the three most common pieces of a crypto portfolio. Bitcoin is the oldest and best-known coin, which is why many people use it as the base of the core. Ethereum is a platform on which applications run, and its role is different: it is a bet on how that platform is used, with more variables along the way. Stablecoins are tokens, generally tied to a currency such as the dollar. They try to keep a stable value, but they are not money in your bank account, and they carry risks of their own. Each one answers a different question. Do not throw them all in the same bag.

cenas.titulo: Rebalancing and the reserve pot
cenas.fala: A portfolio moves on its own. One coin rises, another falls, and the split you wrote three months ago no longer exists. What do you do about it?

cenas.titulo: It is called drift.
cenas.fala: It is called drift. Illustrative example: you started with seventy per cent in Bitcoin, twenty in Ethereum and ten in stablecoins. A year later, Bitcoin has risen a lot and you have eighty per cent. Ethereum and the stablecoins have fallen to twelve and eight. Nobody gave you a signal. The portfolio simply changed shape. Rebalancing is the act of going back to the split you wrote down, using a rule you defined beforehand, and not the mood of the day. It is not a guess about what is going to happen. It is keeping the risk you chose.

cenas.texto: calendar: once a quarter
cenas.fala: There are two simple ways to rebalance. The first is by calendar: once a quarter, you review the split and correct whatever has drifted. The second is by band: you only act when a part drifts further than a certain number of points from its target. Illustrative example: a five-point band. If the core is written as seventy, you act only if it leaves sixty-five or seventy-five. Each method has its advantages. The calendar is simpler to follow. The band only reacts when the drift is real. Choose one, write it in the notebook and keep to it, with no exceptions invented on the spot.

cenas.titulo: Now the reserve pot, which you already know from module seven.
itens: It is the part of the plan's money that was not spent in a given week.
It does not disappear and it is not lost: it is kept aside, and it has one use only.
The ceiling comes first.
cenas.fala: Now the reserve pot, which you already know from module seven. It is the part of the plan's money that was not spent in a given week. It does not disappear and it is not lost: it is kept aside, and it has one use only. Topping up in weeks when the MTM Smart DCA label is Strong Buy, within the monthly ceiling. The ceiling comes first. The pot is not a second account to spend freely. That is why it has to be in the notebook, with a balance and an exit rule, so that it is never an improvised decision.

cenas.titulo: The exit rule is the most important part, and you write it down before you need it.
itens: Illustrative example, of course.
If the market is euphoric, the pot stays still.
cenas.fala: The exit rule is the most important part, and you write it down before you need it. For example: the pot is only used in Strong Buy weeks, and never for more than half of its balance at once. Illustrative example, of course. And there is another rule that is never broken: the pot is never used to buy what has risen sharply. If the market is euphoric, the pot stays still. When you use the pot, record the week, the asset and the reason on the same Friday ritual sheet, so that the saved money always has a history you can account for.

cenas.texto: Rebalancing is not guessing.
cenas.fala: A common confusion: rebalancing is not an attempt to guess the top or the bottom. When you sell a little of what has risen to get back to the split, you are not saying the price is going to fall. You are keeping the risk you chose. And when you buy what has fallen to restore the split, you are not saying it will rise. You are respecting the plan. Rebalancing also has costs: platform fees, possible taxes, which we will look at at the end of the programme, and the work of recording everything. So do not rebalance every week, and always confirm the conditions on your authorised platform.

cenas.texto: date · split before · split after · reason
cenas.fala: Five-minute exercise. Write your rebalancing rule in the notebook: calendar or band, and the value. Then create your pot: one line with the starting balance, which can perfectly well be zero. Write the exit rule in one sentence, and keep the notebook. You do not have to rebalance today. You have to know, before you need to, what you would do. That is what separates a plan from a wish. If you do not know which to choose, start with the calendar, because it is the easiest to keep in a busy week. Notice that you are not choosing the best rule in the world. You are choosing one you are going to respect.

cenas.titulo: Bitcoin has risen and your split has changed. Do you sell to restore it?
cenas.texto: it depends on the rule you wrote. If you have a calendar or a band, you follow the rule and do not decide by the chart of the day.

Another person's assets, or the house's, are the context of that portfolio, and your context is different: a different base amount, a different time horizon, a different tolerance for falls. Copying someone else's context is the fastest way to buy at the wrong bottom without understanding why. Once the distinction is clear, the house portfolio stops being a mirror of ambition and becomes a mirror of method.

Write the answers with the date beside them, because in a few months you will want to compare your reading today with the one you make when you have more experience.

cenas.titulo: Weekly Momentum
cenas.fala: A daily chart shows the week that has passed. The weekly chart shows the year. If you only look at one of them, you are seeing half the film.

cenas.texto: Today we are going to read Momentum on the weekly chart.
cenas.aviso: Educational content. Not financial advice. The risk of loss is real.
cenas.fala: Today we are going to read Momentum on the weekly chart. You already know the five confirmations: the cloud present and in the right colour, the cloud on the right side of the candles, the exponential moving average in agreement, the volume in the colour of the direction, and the RSI crossing in the right zone. On the weekly chart, each candle is a whole week. That changes the rhythm of the reading. A weekly reading does not change from Friday to Monday. So it is a background frame, not a button. Anyone who reads the weekly chart every morning is looking for noise under a magnifying glass. And the risk of loss is real, on any chart, and it always stays with you.

cenas.titulo: Read the confirmations the way you read them on the daily chart, but with more patience.
cenas.fala: Read the confirmations the way you read them on the daily chart, but with more patience. Five out of five, in green: the long-term trend is in favour. Four out of five is still a useful reading. Three or fewer: the weekly chart does not have a strong opinion, and that is also information. The question you ask is simple: does the weekly chart confirm what the daily chart is saying? If the daily is green and the weekly is red, that is not a contradiction to resolve in a hurry. It is a sign that the fall may not be over, and that the pot should be used with more calm, not more haste.

cenas.titulo: turned to buy after a long fall
cenas.fala: Let us go through three typical scenarios. First: the weekly chart has turned green after a long fall. It is a good moment to confirm that the pot is ready, because Strong Buy weeks may come next. Second: strong red for several weeks. Here the rule is the same as in module seven: base always, and the pot kept still until the weekly chart starts to ease. Third: lilac boxes on the weekly chart, a sideways market. For the DCA, it is a period to accumulate with patience, with no hurry to use the pot. In none of these three cases does the weekly chart stop the DCA. It only helps you decide the size.

cenas.texto: weekly: once a month
cenas.fala: Now the rhythm, which is the part most people get wrong. You read the weekly chart once a month, on a quiet weekend, to see the whole picture and review your plan. You read the daily chart every Friday, within your ritual. The weekly reading does not replace the daily one: the weekly sets the context, and the daily decides the day. If you ever catch yourself opening the weekly chart every morning, stop, breathe and go back to the notebook. That is anxiety dressed up as analysis, and it costs a lot in hasty decisions.

cenas.titulo: The weekly gives you the map, not the timetable.

cartoes.d: A common mistake is looking on the weekly chart for the exact day to buy.
That day does not exist.
It does not tell you whether tomorrow is the best day for anything.

cenas.fala: A common mistake is looking on the weekly chart for the exact day to buy. That day does not exist. The weekly chart gives you the map: the direction of the background and the weight of the trend. It does not tell you whether tomorrow is the best day for anything. And there is another trap: changing your plan just because the weekly chart changed colour once. Wait for the change to be confirmed over another one or two candles. If your plan is long term, the weekly chart serves to adjust the size of the pot, and never to stop the DCA. Never.

cenas.texto: did the plan change?
cenas.fala: Three-minute exercise. Open the weekly chart of an asset in your plan, count the five confirmations and write the result in the notebook, with the date. Then write, in one sentence, whether the plan changes or not. If it does not change, write “no change”. It may look like a formality, but it is discipline. Six months from now, you will have a history of readings, not a memory of when you happened to remember. And memory, as you know, tends to side with the story that suits us. If the weekly chart is unreadable to you, that is fine. Write “cannot read it” and ask yourself why. Very often it is a lack of habit, and habit comes with repetition.

cenas.titulo: DEFY as a second opinion
cenas.fala: A second opinion is only worth something if it is not a copy of the first. So let us see what DEFY asks that Momentum does not.

cenas.titulo: You already know DEFY from the earlier lessons.
cenas.fala: You already know DEFY from the earlier lessons. It draws exhaustion bands around a smooth average: an inner one, a middle one and an outer one. The question DEFY asks is a different one. While Momentum asks whether the direction is in favour, DEFY asks whether the move has already gone too far. These are different questions, which is why they can disagree. When they disagree, nothing is broken. There is information. And that information is worth more than a forced agreement. We are not going to repeat everything you saw in module seven. We are going to look at DEFY as an extra reading, which comes after Momentum, not before it.

cenas.titulo: The stars count the confirmations: has the level already reacted before?
cenas.fala: When the price reaches the outer band and turns with a strong candle, DEFY may mark an idea. The stars count the confirmations: has the level already reacted before? Is the trend cloud on the same side? Is there a volume break? Three confirmations give one star, more give two or three, and when everything lines up the candle turns gold. The stars measure how many confirmations there are. They do not measure the certainty of the result, because that does not exist. A gold candle is not a guarantee of a rise. It is a stretched price with many pieces fitting together, and that is all it is.

cenas.titulo: Momentum green with 4 or 5 · DEFY with stars

cartoes.d: Let us go through the combinations.
Momentum green and DEFY with stars: both readings in favour.
If the MTM Smart DCA label also helps, it is a week to use the pot with judgement.

cenas.fala: Let us go through the combinations. Momentum green and DEFY with stars: both readings in favour. If the MTM Smart DCA label also helps, it is a week to use the pot with judgement. Momentum green and DEFY without stars: one reading in favour. Momentum red or lilac with stars on DEFY: also one reading in favour, because a buy idea exists, but the trend does not yet agree. And Momentum red or lilac without stars: no reading in favour, and the base is enough. Notice that there is no row that says “buy everything”. That row does not exist, and if you find it in some group or other, be suspicious of it.

cartoes.d: Let us put this into a simple frame, to stick next to the screen.
Two readings in favour: base plus pot, within the ceiling.
One reading in favour: base plus, at most, half the pot.

cenas.fala: Let us put this into a simple frame, to stick next to the screen. Two readings in favour: base plus pot, within the ceiling. One reading in favour: base plus, at most, half the pot. None: only the base. Above everything sits the monthly ceiling, which is never breached, and the MTM Smart DCA label, which gives the starting point. DEFY is a second opinion. It is not the first criterion, and it has no power to cancel the label. It helps you choose how much of the pot to use, and that is all. Print it or copy it by hand, and always keep it in front of you on Friday, so that the decision does not depend on who is most tired that day.

cenas.titulo: DEFY signals are for trading. In DCA, they only affect the size.
itens: Repeat after me: DEFY signals were designed for trading.
They carry an entry, a stop and targets, because that is what a trader needs.
In DCA you do not use those levels.
cenas.fala: Repeat after me: DEFY signals were designed for trading. They carry an entry, a stop and targets, because that is what a trader needs. In DCA you do not use those levels. You do not buy at the “entry price”, you do not place a stop and you do not take profit at targets. Your DCA is long term, and DEFY only affects the size of the top-up. If one day you want to trade with rules, that is a different path, with different training, a different account and a different risk. It is not this one. And having DEFY on the screen does not give your DCA a stop.

Write down the two readings and the decision: base, base plus half the pot, or base plus the pot, always within the ceiling. Do this for a week, without buying anything extra. You will see that the two tools disagree more often than you imagined, and that the disagreement teaches more than agreement does. If there are no stars in any week, that is also a valid reading. Record that there was no idea and follow the plan, without looking for a star that is not there.

cenas.titulo: Sentiment, fear and euphoria, and BTC dominance
cenas.fala: You have heard someone say “there is fear in the market” or “this is euphoric”. It sounds like information. But what actually changes in your plan? Let us find out.

cenas.titulo: public sentiment indices · context, not a signal
itens: Sentiment is the collective mood.
There are public indices that try to measure whether people are frightened or greedy.
Zero is extreme fear; one hundred is extreme euphoria.
cenas.fala: Sentiment is the collective mood. There are public indices that try to measure whether people are frightened or greedy. They usually combine several signals, for example volatility and public attention to the topic, and present the result on a scale from zero to one hundred. Zero is extreme fear; one hundred is extreme euphoria. Notice the words: these indices are constructions. They are not the market. They are a snapshot of how people feel about the market. Before you use any of them, read on its own page how it is built. Useful for context, but never a command.
cenas.cap: Sentiment, fear and euphoria, and BTC dominance
Sentiment, fear and euphoria, and BTC dominance
cenas.texto: the number does not change the top-up
cenas.fala: Why do fear and euphoria matter? Because people's behaviour tends to get worse at the extremes: they buy more at the top and sell more at the bottom. DCA was designed precisely to escape that trap. So sentiment does not tell you how much to buy for the base. It tells you where you stand in the collective emotion. Extreme fear is a good moment to remember the written plan. Extreme euphoria is a good moment to remember the ceiling. In neither case does the DCA stop, and in neither case does the index number by itself change the top-up.

cenas.kicker: context in the notebook, not on the button
cenas.titulo: BTC dominance = Bitcoin's share of the total crypto market value
cenas.fala: Now Bitcoin dominance. It is the share Bitcoin occupies in the total value of the crypto market. Illustrative example: if the whole market were worth one hundred, and Bitcoin were worth fifty, dominance would be fifty per cent. When dominance rises, it usually means that money is concentrating in Bitcoin and that the smaller coins suffer more. When it falls, the opposite can happen, with the smaller coins gaining ground. These are patterns that are observed, not laws. You never know how long they last, and you never know whether they repeat in the same form.

cenas.titulo: Taking profit with written rules
cenas.fala: Almost everyone knows how to buy. Very few know when to sell, and even fewer know why they sold. Today we write that down before we need it.

cenas.texto: First, the warning that will appear whenever we touch money: educational content.
cenas.aviso: Educational content. Not financial advice. The risk of loss is real.
cenas.fala: First, the warning that will appear whenever we touch money: educational content. The risk of loss is real, and in crypto it can be total. With that said, let us go to a question that almost nobody answers seriously: when do you take profit? Many people only think about it once the price has already risen or already fallen, and then the decision is emotional. Greed on one side, fear on the other. The idea of this lesson is simple: the decision to sell has to be taken on a calm day, on paper, with rules you wrote beforehand. When the market accelerates, it is not the time to think. It is the time to carry out what you have already decided.

cenas.titulo: We call this a profit-taking ladder.
cenas.fala: We call this a profit-taking ladder. Each rung is a level of gain, measured against your average purchase price. On each rung you sell a fixed part of the position, and the rest stays with you. Notice what this does: the part you sell is converted into euros, and the part you keep continues to take part if the market keeps rising. It is not a magic formula, and it does not tell you when the top arrives. It only tells you what you will do on each rung, before the rung is reached. That is what takes the drama out of the decision.

cartoes.d: I will give you an illustrative example, just so you can see the mechanics.
Imagine a position with an average price of one hundred.
On the first rung, at plus fifty per cent, you sell a fifth of the position.

cenas.fala: I will give you an illustrative example, just so you can see the mechanics. Imagine a position with an average price of one hundred. On the first rung, at plus fifty per cent, you sell a fifth of the position. On the second rung, at plus one hundred per cent, you sell another fifth. On the third, at plus two hundred per cent, you sell one more fifth. What is left stays with you, under its own rule. The numbers are mine, chosen for the example. They are not a forecast, not a target and not a recommendation. You choose your own rungs and your own percentages, according to your plan and your tolerance for risk. What matters is that they are written down.

cenas.texto: rung · part · date
cenas.fala: Each rung has three pieces of information, and all three have to be written down. First: the rung, as a percentage against your average price. Second: the part, as a fraction of your position and not in euros, so the rule still makes sense when the position changes. Third: the date or the condition for review. For example, I review the ladder on the first Friday of every month. If there is neither a date nor a condition, the rule does not exist, it is just a wish. And there is one thing the ladder does not replace: the DCA. Purchases still happen on your day, as in module seven. Selling a part is a separate decision, with its own role.

cenas.texto: What is not written down does not exist.
cenas.fala: There are three mistakes I see often, and the ladder prevents them. The first is changing the rule halfway, because the price is running and you want to see more. The second is selling everything at once out of fear, on a day of panic, and then watching the rise without your part. The third is selling nothing and calling that patience, when in fact it is a lack of plan. With the ladder written down, any of these mistakes has to go through paper first. That alone gives you a pause. And in fast markets, a pause is worth more than it seems.

cenas.titulo: Five-minute exercise, to do today.
itens: Take your notebook and write your ladder for one position in your plan.
Three rungs are enough.
For each one, write the rung, the part and the review date.
cenas.fala: Five-minute exercise, to do today. Take your notebook and write your ladder for one position in your plan. Three rungs are enough. For each one, write the rung, the part and the review date. You do not have to get it right. You have to write it down, and do it calmly, without the screen open beside you. Then keep the sheet next to the plan from module seven, so the two can be read together. Next lesson we talk about what to do when the market does not rise, but falls in a brutal way, and why that plan also has to be written down before it is needed.

cenas.texto: no. It only defines what you sell on each rung, and the DCA stays separate.
cenas.fala: Does the ladder force you to buy more when the price rises? no. It only defines what you sell on each rung, and the DCA stays separate.

cenas.titulo: What to do in a crash: the plan written beforehand
cenas.fala: A day of heavy falls does not look like a crisis. It looks like a notification, a friend calling and a finger that wants to press sell. That is why the plan has to be written beforehand.

cenas.titulo: Plan written beforehand.
cenas.fala: Large falls happen in crypto. I am not going to tell you when or how big, because I do not know, and nobody knows. What I do know is that they happen often enough to deserve a plan. And the moment when decisions are most often made badly is precisely the moment of the fall, when the screen is red, the conversations are in panic and the brain wants to do something, anything, right now. The solution is not to have more courage in the moment. It is to have fewer decisions to make in that moment. That is why we write the plan today, when we are calm, and not tomorrow, when it is already on fire.
cenas.cap: What to do in a crash: the plan written beforehand

cenas.titulo: three parts, one page

cartoes.d: The plan for a crash has three parts.
Before: what you already have set up.
After: when and how you review the strategy.

cenas.fala: The plan for a crash has three parts. Before: what you already have set up. Your base amount, your monthly ceiling, your reserve pot and the alerts switched on in the app. During: what you do in each band of decline, written with the same logic as the MTM Smart DCA, in which the Strong Buy label changes the size of the top-up and does not tell you to stop. After: when and how you review the strategy. One page is enough. If it does not fit on one page, it is still being thought out too much, and on the day of the fall nobody reads twenty.
cenas.cap: What to do in a crash: the plan written beforehand

cenas.kicker: the DCA never stops, it only adjusts
cenas.titulo: Now the during, which is the heart of the plan.
cenas.fala: Now the during, which is the heart of the plan. For each band of decline, you write the action. For example, illustrative example: if the asset falls more than thirty per cent against your average price, the DCA continues on the base. If the pot has money, you use part of it, within the ceiling, as module seven teaches. You do not sell anything in that band. Notice this carefully: the DCA never stops, it only changes size. A fall does not give you permission to stop buying, and it does not oblige you to buy more than the ceiling allows. If your strategy has a position you genuinely want to sell in a fall, that is a separate written rule, with its own condition.
cenas.cap: What to do in a crash: the plan written beforehand

cenas.titulo: There is one rule that should be in every crash plan: the pause.
itens: When something makes you want to sell outside the plan, you wait twenty-four hours.
It is not a punishment, it is a filter.
A great deal of panic decisions disappear within twenty-four hours.
cenas.fala: There is one rule that should be in every crash plan: the pause. When something makes you want to sell outside the plan, you wait twenty-four hours. It is not a punishment, it is a filter. A great deal of panic decisions disappear within twenty-four hours. If after the pause you still think the sale makes sense, write down why, with the condition that justifies it, and check whether it matches the rule you wrote for the crash. If it does not match, keep to the plan. And switch off price notifications during the day of the fall. Looking at the chart every five minutes does not help you think. It only gives you the feeling that you are doing something.
cenas.cap: What to do in a crash: the plan written beforehand

cenas.texto: Nobody will remind you of the plan for you.
cenas.fala: I will tell you this plainly: in a fall, the people around you will say things. Some will tell you to sell everything, others to buy everything, and others will show charts that look like certainties. None of them has your table. That is why the plan stays written and signed by you, kept where you can see it. If you only have it in your head, in a fall your head will tell you whatever it likes. Also write down the contact of one trusted person who can remind you of the plan. Not to decide for you. To remind you of what you decided when you were calm.

cenas.titulo: Advanced security: copies, metal and places
cenas.fala: Your seed is your entire account. And the worst thing you can do to it is not to lose it on an unlucky day. It is to leave it where someone can look at it at their leisure.

cenas.texto: In lesson four we talked about your seed, the words that give access to your coins.
cenas.fala: In lesson four we talked about your seed, the words that give access to your coins. Now we go one level up, because when the value grows, the risk changes shape. There are two threats that weigh the same: losing the seed, and someone else getting hold of it. Any security plan has to deal with both. The rule that is not negotiable is this: the seed never exists in digital form. Not a photo, not a note on your phone, not an email to yourself, not a file in the cloud, not a password manager. Any of these can be copied, synced or stolen, and all of that can happen without you noticing anything.
cenas.cap: Advanced security: copies, metal and places
Advanced security: copies, metal and places
cenas.texto: paper burns · metal endures
cenas.fala: If it is not digital, is it paper? It can be, but paper is fragile. It burns, it gets wet, it breaks down over time, and a house move can throw away a folded sheet in a drawer. That is why the most solid option is metal: a plate or a holder where the words are engraved or punched, resistant to fire and water. Using paper as the first copy is not a mistake, as long as the metal copy follows. The goal is for the information to survive a fire, a flood or a day when your home is turned upside down.

cenas.titulo: two copies · two places
itens: Now the rule about copies.
Two copies, in two different places.
Not the same drawer, not the same safe, not the same house.
cenas.fala: Now the rule about copies. Two copies, in two different places. Not the same drawer, not the same safe, not the same house. If a fire or a burglary takes one, the other is still there. One option is a safe at home, well hidden and fixed to the structure. The other can be a safe in a trusted place, outside the home. There is no perfect place. There are places where the risk of loss is low and the risk of improper access is also low. Choose with that balance in mind, and write in the plan where each copy is.
cenas.cap: Advanced security: copies, metal and places
Advanced security: copies, metal and places
cenas.texto: No legitimate support asks for the seed.
cenas.fala: A rule that sounds obvious and that many people break: nobody asks you for the seed. No legitimate support service, no authorised platform, no person saying they are from support asks for the words. If anyone asks, even if the request comes with a beautiful logo, an urgent message or a friendly phone call, the answer is no. And do not write it down on any website, in any third-party app, or for a friend who is helping you set something up. The seed is only used at the moment of restoring your wallet, in a place you control. Afterwards it goes back to the paper copy and the metal one.

cenas.texto: Test, do not copy.
cenas.fala: How do you know the copy works? You do not open it to check, because every time you expose it there is a small exposure. What you do is a restore test, in a new, empty wallet, with none of your main value, following the procedure you already know from module four. If the test works, the copy is good. If it does not, you find out now, and not on the day you need it. Do this test once a year, or whenever you change wallets. And never put the copies together in one photo, one folder or one envelope.
cenas.cap: Advanced security: copies, metal and places

cenas.titulo: Mission for this lesson, to do this week: check your seed against four questions.
itens: Is it free of any digital format?
Do you have two copies?
Are they in two different places?
And have you done the restore test in a new wallet?
cenas.fala: Mission for this lesson, to do this week: check your seed against four questions. Is it free of any digital format? Do you have two copies? Are they in two different places? And have you done the restore test in a new wallet? If the answer to any of these is no, that is where the work is. It is not glamorous, but it is what separates someone who loses a phone from someone who loses access to their coins. In the last lesson of this module we talk about what happens to your seed and your coins when you are no longer around to look after them.
cenas.cap: Advanced security: copies, metal and places

cenas.titulo: Can you keep a photo of the seed on your phone “just for safety”?

cenas.fala: Can you keep a photo of the seed on your phone “just for safety”? no. Any digital copy can be copied or synced, so no.

cenas.titulo: Crypto inheritance and the level 2 mission
cenas.fala: Nobody likes to think about this. But if your coins exist only in your head, when you are gone, they are missing for the people you love too. This has a solution, and it is simpler than it sounds.

cenas.texto: Crypto inheritance plan
cenas.fala: Let us go to inheritance. This is the last security point of level two, and it is the one most people put off. The idea is simple: someone you trust needs to be able to understand what exists, where it is and how to access it, when you can no longer do so. You do not need to give them the seed, neither now nor ever. What you give them is a map. A map says that you have crypto, in which types of wallet and on which authorised platforms, what the copies are, where they are kept and whom to ask for help finding them. Written this way, the map protects your family and does not expose your coins.
cenas.cap: Crypto inheritance and the level 2 mission
Crypto inheritance and the level 2 mission
cenas.texto: the map without the key
cenas.fala: Separate the information into three parts. The map: what you have and where it is, with no access words. The seed copies, which are the key, stay in the safe places from the previous lesson, and never in the same envelope as the map. And the contacts: who is the trusted lawyer or notary to ask how this works in your case, and who is the person who will read the map when it is needed. The golden rule is that no single part, on its own, gives access to your coins. Whoever reads the map does not have the key. Whoever has the key does not know what it opens. The two have to come together.

cenas.texto: Talk to a professional
cenas.fala: An honest note about the legal side. Inheritance rules vary from country to country, and they vary even more when the assets are digital. I am not going to tell you here what the law provides for your case, because that depends on your situation and on who will inherit. What I ask is that, before you consider your plan finished, you talk to a lawyer or a trusted notary. Take the map, without the access words, and ask how it should be drafted to be valid. And if you live or have assets in another country, ask about that one too. This is not legal advice. It is a warning not to leave the subject for later.
cenas.cap: Crypto inheritance and the level 2 mission

cenas.titulo: Second, the DCA alerts switched on in the MTM System app, in the settings.
itens: Four lines, one per week.
cenas.fala: Now the level two mission, which brings together everything you did in modules seven to ten. First, your written DCA plan, with the fixed monthly ceiling and the reserve pot, on a single sheet. It has the base amount, the assets, the top-up day, the size rules with the MTM Smart DCA table and what happens to the money you do not spend. Second, the DCA alerts switched on in the MTM System app, in the settings. Third, the Friday ritual carried out four weeks in a row, with a record of each one in the notebook. If on a Friday you do not buy, you still do the ritual and record what you would have done. Four lines, one per week.
cenas.cap: Crypto inheritance and the level 2 mission

cenas.texto: 4 Fridays · 4 records
cenas.fala: Why four weeks and not one? Because one week is a coincidence. Four weeks in a row are a habit beginning. And it is in habit that DCA works, not on the day it went well or badly. Notice also what I am not asking of you: I am not asking you to have got it right, or to have made a profit. I am asking that the process has happened four times, at the same time and on the same sheet. If one Friday is missed for a real reason, such as a trip or an illness, it is not a failure. You restart the count and carry on. What you cannot do is pretend the record exists when it does not.

cenas.texto: Level 2 mission: plan, alerts, four recorded Fridays.
cenas.fala: Level two mission, in short: a written DCA plan with ceiling and pot, DCA alerts switched on, and four consecutive Fridays of recorded ritual. It is not measured by what the market did. It is measured by whether you did it. And inheritance comes in here too, in the form of a map, with the key kept separate. Remember the essentials: this is educational content, not financial advice. The risk of loss is real, and the MTM tools help you decide with information. They do not decide for you. Level three brings in perpetuals, which are a different game. Before we get there, the plan for this level has to be done.

cenas.titulo: What a perpetual is, and funding
cenas.fala: A perpetual is a contract that never expires. It sounds simple, and the part that does not expire is exactly the part that will cost you attention.

cenas.texto: The risk of loss is real.
cenas.aviso: Educational content. Not financial advice. The risk of loss is real.
cenas.fala: Before any numbers, the warning that will be on screen throughout this module: educational content. The risk of loss is real. With perpetuals you can lose everything you put up as margin, and that happens faster than most people think. This module is for understanding, not for starting. Level three is optional. And before any real euro, what counts is the simulated account, as you have known since the start of the bootcamp. With that said, let us look at what a perpetual is. I want you to leave here with one clear sentence.
cenas.cap: What a perpetual is, and funding
What a perpetual is, and funding
cenas.texto: perpetual = no date
cenas.fala: A normal futures contract has an expiry date. At the end of that date it is settled, and that is the end of it. A perpetual has no such date. It stays open for as long as you want it to, and as long as you have margin to keep it open. To stay close to the spot price, the perpetual uses a mechanism called funding. It is not a brokerage fee. It is a payment that happens from time to time, between those who are long and those who are short. When the perpetual trades above the spot price, those who are long pay those who are short. When it trades below, the opposite happens. It is the part most people ignore, and it weighs more than it seems on positions that stay open for days.

cenas.kicker: you pay while the position is open

cenas.fala: Let us look at an illustrative example. You have a long position with one thousand euros of notional value, which is the total size of the position, not the money you put in. The funding is zero point zero five per cent per payment period. Per period, you pay fifty cents. If the funding is positive, those who are long pay. If it is negative, those who are long receive. The number is only there to make the sum, and funding changes over time. What matters is the mechanism: someone who stays in a position for a long time with the funding working against them pays a small amount every day, and that does not show up on the candlestick chart.

cenas.titulo: perpetual vs spot price
cenas.fala: Why does the perpetual stay close to the spot price? Because funding pushes. When there are many people long and the perpetual trades above the real price, funding turns positive, and those who are long pay to keep their position. That tends to cool demand on the long side. The reverse happens when many people are short: funding turns negative, and the shorts are the ones who pay. It is not magic, it is an incentive. In practice, funding is a cost or an income that runs while the position is open, and its sign changes with the market's conditions.

cenas.titulo: Isolated margin and cross margin
cenas.fala: Two accounts with the same balance can react in completely different ways to the same fall. The difference lies in a choice that almost nobody reads.

cenas.kicker: cross: the risk belongs to the whole account
cenas.titulo: margin: what protects you and what puts you at risk
itens: Margin is the money you put up to hold the position.
It is not the cost of the whole position, it is the collateral.
There are two ways to organise it: isolated and cross.
cenas.fala: Margin is the money you put up to hold the position. It is not the cost of the whole position, it is the collateral. When you open a leveraged perpetual, the platform requires an initial margin, and it is that margin which rises and falls with the market. There are two ways to organise it: isolated and cross. The difference is not in the leverage. It is in who pays when the position goes wrong. This choice sounds technical, but it is one of the most important risk decisions in this module, and it is often the one people make without thinking.

cenas.titulo: Isolated margin means each position has its own collateral.
itens: If you put one hundred euros into a position, only those one hundred euros are at risk.
Cross margin means all positions share the available balance.
A position in trouble can use the money from the others to hold on.
cenas.fala: Isolated margin means each position has its own collateral. If you put one hundred euros into a position, only those one hundred euros are at risk. If the position is liquidated, you lose those hundred, and the rest of the account stays intact. Cross margin means all positions share the available balance. A position in trouble can use the money from the others to hold on. It sounds like an advantage, and sometimes it is, but it has a cost: a single bad position can drag the entire account down. For someone learning, that is a big problem.

cenas.kicker: isolated: the risk stays in the position
cenas.titulo: isolated: limit per position · cross: shares the balance

cartoes.t: isolated: the risk stays in the position
cartoes.d: Let us put the two side by side, with an illustrative example.

cartoes.t: cross: the risk belongs to the whole account
cartoes.d: You have a simulated account of one thousand euros and open two positions.
With isolated margin, you give one hundred euros to each.

cenas.fala: Let us put the two side by side, with an illustrative example. You have a simulated account of one thousand euros and open two positions. With isolated margin, you give one hundred euros to each. If the first goes wrong and is liquidated, you lose those hundred, and the second carries on with its hundred. With cross margin, both use the full balance of one thousand. If the first goes wrong, the second can use what is left, and liquidation only happens when the whole account reaches the limit. In other words, cross holds out for longer, but when it fails, it fails all together. The numbers are for the account, not for any real position.

cenas.texto: Cross does not protect you. It only delays.
cenas.fala: This is my view, which you can argue with: for someone starting out, isolated margin is the choice I recommend. Someone starting has not yet tested a risk plan, and isolated forces you to decide how much each position gets. That limit is a lesson in itself. With cross, the account works like one single pot, and it is easy to give more margin to a position that is losing, in the hope that it recovers. That is called putting more money into something that is already going wrong. Cross has its place for those who already have written and tested rules, but it is not where you start.

If it does not allow it, do it on paper. Fill in the sheet: how much money is inside each position, what happens to the other one if the first goes wrong, and which of the two leaves you more at ease. There is no right answer to the last question, only yours. Next lesson we see what liquidation is and how it is calculated, in simplified form, with an illustrative sum.

cenas.texto: the balance of the other positions, and so the risk becomes the risk of the whole account.
cenas.fala: With cross margin, what can a position with problems use to hold on? the balance of the other positions, and so the risk becomes the risk of the whole account.

cenas.titulo: Liquidation, with an illustrative sum
cenas.fala: Liquidation is the moment when the platform closes your position because there is no longer enough collateral. Nobody asks you. It just happens.

cenas.texto: Let us work through the liquidation sum step by step, with an illustrative sum.
cenas.fala: Let us work through the liquidation sum step by step, with an illustrative sum. It is not anyone's actual account. These are round numbers, so you can see the mechanics. Imagine a simulated account with five hundred euros of margin on a long position, with ten times leverage. Ten times means the position has a notional value of five thousand euros. The five hundred is your collateral, the five thousand is the size of the bet. This difference is the centre of this lesson. And notice: the example is illustrative, and the platform you use may have different numbers and different rules.

cenas.texto: margin being consumed
cenas.fala: When the price moves against your position, the loss comes out of the margin. With five thousand of notional, every one per cent move against you is worth fifty euros. If the price falls ten per cent, you lose five hundred, and the margin drops to zero. In a simplified account, that is where liquidation happens: when the loss consumes the margin. But this is a simplification, and the difference matters. In practice, the platform requires a minimum maintenance margin, and it liquidates before the margin reaches zero. So the real liquidation price sits a little closer to the entry than the simple sum says.

cenas.kicker: leverage shortens the margin for error
cenas.titulo: entry 100 · simplified liquidation ≈ 90 · illustrative example

cartoes.d: Imagine the position is long with an entry at one hundred.
Notice the logic behind it: roughly one divided by the leverage.
Ten times gives ten per cent.

cenas.fala: Now the price. Imagine the position is long with an entry at one hundred. With this simplified sum, the liquidation sits near ninety, because a ten per cent fall is what the five hundred of margin can absorb against the five thousand of notional. Notice the logic behind it: roughly one divided by the leverage. Ten times gives ten per cent. Twenty times gives five per cent. The higher the leverage, the shorter the distance to liquidation. In other words, leverage does not buy you more time. It shortens your margin for error. This figure is an illustrative example, and it is not a rule for any position.

cenas.texto: Liquidation is not a number. It is a date that arrives without warning.
cenas.fala: And now the point I want you to keep. Liquidation does not warn you. There is no moment when the platform tells you it is about to close, and there is no guarantee that the price stops exactly at the value you calculated. In a fast market, with one long candle and suddenly, the price can pass the liquidation level in seconds, and the close happens at whatever price there is at that moment, which can be worse than the number you wrote down. So the liquidation price you see on screen is a reference limit, not a protection. Protection, if it exists, is somewhere else: it is the stop, which we will look at later in this level.

cenas.texto: Recalculate before you open.
cenas.fala: Mission for this lesson: take an illustrative account, in a simulation, and calculate the simplified liquidation for three leverage levels, five, ten and twenty. Write down the percentage distance to the liquidation price in each case. Then check it on the panel of the platform you use, if it has one. If the numbers do not match, look for the difference, which is usually in the maintenance margin and the fees. Do not open any real position to do this calculation, not even out of curiosity. Next lesson we talk about costs, which is where the sum usually turns out to be more expensive than it looks.

cenas.texto: it moves closer to the entry, because the same collateral supports a larger notional.
cenas.fala: With the same margin of five hundred euros, what happens to the liquidation price when you move from ten to twenty times? it moves closer to the entry, because the same collateral supports a larger notional.

cenas.titulo: Fees and the real cost
cenas.fala: A trade can look as though it went well, and once you do the sum on the fees, nothing is left. This lesson is about the sums nobody does in front of the screen.

cenas.texto: Let us talk about money that leaves without being seen.
cenas.fala: Let us talk about money that leaves without being seen. With perpetuals there are at least three kinds of cost. The opening fee, the closing fee and the funding we have already seen. There is also a hidden cost, which is the spread, the difference between the buy price and the sell price at that moment. Each one is small, but added up and multiplied by the leverage and by how often you trade, they can eat a large part of what you thought you had. This invoice is illustrative, with no values from any particular platform. Your authorised platform has its own fee tables, and you have to read them before you open anything.

cenas.titulo: The fee depends on how you enter.
cenas.fala: The fee depends on how you enter. When you place an order that waits in the order book, and is not executed straight away, you usually pay a lower fee, called maker. When the order executes immediately and takes liquidity from the market, you pay a higher fee, the taker fee. Platforms vary, so check the fee menu of your authorised platform before you open, for each type of order. Also ask yourself whether the order type you are using is the one you want, and not simply the fastest one to click.

cenas.titulo: notional €5,000 · fee of 0.05% per side · illustrative example

cartoes.d: Illustrative example, with round numbers.
Opening costs two euros and fifty cents.
Closing costs another two euros and fifty cents.

cenas.fala: Illustrative example, with round numbers. A notional of five thousand euros, and a fee of zero point zero five per cent on each side of the trade, opening and closing. Opening costs two euros and fifty cents. Closing costs another two euros and fifty cents. Total, five euros, on a trade of five thousand. That seems little. Now look at the margin: five hundred euros. Five euros on five hundred is one per cent of the collateral, in fees alone, before the market has moved. If you repeat this trade ten times with the same margin, that is fifty euros, ten per cent of the collateral, going to the platform. None of those fifty euros appears on the chart.

cenas.texto: fee cost for the size of the account
cenas.fala: This is where the account panel of Aurum Flow Cripto helps. It shows the notional, the useful leverage and the fee cost for the size of your account, before you open anything. The question you should always ask is this: if the trade does exactly what the plan says, how much is left after the fees? If the answer is almost nothing, the trade may not be worth the effort, however good it looks on the chart. This is not a guarantee of anything. It is a sum done in your head, and it protects you from an illusion.

cenas.titulo: Five-minute exercise, on paper.
itens: What is the notional?
How much does opening cost?
Two euros and fifty cents.
cenas.fala: Five-minute exercise, on paper. A margin of one thousand euros, leverage of five times, and a fee of zero point zero five per cent per side. What is the notional? Five thousand. How much does opening cost? Two euros and fifty cents. How much does closing cost? Another two euros and fifty cents. What is the total cost, as a percentage of the margin? Half a per cent. Now repeat it with leverage of twenty times, keeping the same margin. You do not need to get your platform's fee exactly right. You need to understand that the cost rises with the notional, not with the margin you put in. Next lesson we look at the most important part of this module: why leverage does not change the right risk.

cenas.titulo: Why do fees rise when you increase the leverage, with the same margin?
cenas.texto: because the fee is calculated on the notional, and the notional rises with the leverage.
cenas.fala: Why do fees rise when you increase the leverage, with the same margin? because the fee is calculated on the notional, and the notional rises with the leverage.

cenas.titulo: Leverage does not change the right risk
cenas.fala: Leverage sounds like an accelerator. But if it were only an accelerator, what would stop the car? The answer is the stop and the size of the position, not the number on the screen.

cenas.texto: Risk is defined by the stop and the size
cenas.fala: We have reached the lesson that sums up level three, and perhaps the most important one in the module. When someone tells you they will use five times, or twenty times, the right question is not what the leverage is. The right question is: how much do I lose if the stop is hit? That question has an answer that does not depend on the leverage. It depends on two things: the distance to the stop and the size of the position. Leverage only tells you how much margin you need to hold that position. We will see why, with sums and with illustrative examples, of course.
cenas.cap: Leverage does not change the right risk
Leverage does not change the right risk
cenas.texto: loss = notional × stop distance
cenas.fala: The formula fits on a napkin: the loss, if the stop is hit, equals the notional multiplied by the stop distance as a percentage. That is all. Leverage does not enter into it. What enters is the size of the position, which is the notional, and the point where you are willing to get out. With this, the risk per trade is defined before you open. If you want to lose at most one per cent of your account, you choose the notional and the stop distance so that the loss, in that case, is one per cent. Leverage then becomes a consequence of that choice, not the starting point.

cenas.titulo: account: €1,000 · risk: €10 (1%)
itens: First case: a stop at two per cent from the entry price.
Notional: ten divided by two per cent gives five hundred euros.
Leverage, against the account, half a time.
cenas.fala: Let us take the same account of one thousand euros, with a risk of ten euros per trade, which is one per cent. First case: a stop at two per cent from the entry price. Notional: ten divided by two per cent gives five hundred euros. Leverage, against the account, half a time. Second case: a stop at one per cent. Notional of one thousand euros, leverage of one time. Third case: a stop at half a per cent. Notional of two thousand, leverage of two times. In all three, if the stop is hit, you lose exactly ten euros. What changed was the notional and the leverage, not the risk. This is the point I want you to keep.
cenas.cap: Leverage does not change the right risk
Leverage does not change the right risk
cenas.texto: A stop is not a guarantee.
cenas.fala: An important caveat: the stop is an order, and an order can be executed at a worse price than the one you wrote, if the market makes a sudden jump. In a sharp move, the close can come out further away than the level you marked. So the stop reduces the risk, but does not eliminate it. And liquidation still exists, because if the margin is too small for the stop distance, the platform closes the position before the stop is reached. The rule is not “I set a stop and I can relax”. The rule is: the stop sits far enough away for normal noise, and the position is small enough that a jump does not wipe out your account.

cenas.texto: Level 3: simulated account only, up to 30 trades with a journal.
cenas.fala: Now the level three rule, which is not negotiable. This level is done only in a simulated account, MTM Funded or WebTrader, until you have completed thirty trades with a full journal. Thirty, not three. The journal records the date, the plan, the stop, the notional, the risk in euros, the fee, the reason for entry, the reason for exit and what you learned. Only after thirty trades can you think about a real account, and that decision is yours, never made with rent money. Mission for this lesson: open your simulated account, do the risk calculation with the model from this lesson, record the first lines of the journal, and write at the top of the sheet: zero of thirty.

cenas.titulo: The first house rule: Aurum Flow only trades with the trend.

cenas.titulo: The three-DEMA filter and the momentum confirmation
cenas.fala: Saying 'there is a trend' is easy. Proving it with numbers is another story. Three averages and a strength indicator are there for that.

cenas.titulo: To measure the trend, Aurum Flow uses three DEMA averages, of 15, 50 and 238 periods.
cenas.fala: To measure the trend, Aurum Flow uses three DEMA averages, of 15, 50 and 238 periods. A DEMA lags less than a simple average and reacts faster. The 15 shows the recent move, the 50 the medium term, the 238 the background. When all three are ordered in the same direction and the price is on the same side, the filter says there is a trend. When they are tangled together, the filter says there isn't. And a filter that says "no" is as useful as one that says "yes", because it saves you a bad entry.

cenas.titulo: Notice the difference.
cenas.fala: Notice the difference. On the left, the three averages are ordered, with the fastest on top and the slowest at the bottom, and the price is trading above them. That is an uptrend. On the right, the lines cross each other and the price keeps crossing them from one side to the other. That is sideways. Both are illustrative examples. If you look at ten charts like these, you will see that sideways shows up more often than you would like. With the filter, it is a "no" without drama, not a signal you have to force.
cenas.cap: The three-DEMA filter and the momentum confirmation

cenas.texto: RSI · momentum confirmation
cenas.fala: The trend filter tells you which way to look, but not when. That is where the momentum confirmation comes in, done with the RSI. The RSI measures the recent strength of moves on a scale from zero to one hundred. On a buy entry, we want the RSI to confirm strength in the same direction as the signal, not turn against it. On a sell entry, it is the opposite. There is no magic number here for you to memorize. The rule is the direction: momentum has to be on the side of the trend.
cenas.cap: The three-DEMA filter and the momentum confirmation

cenas.titulo: trend: three DEMA aligned
itens: First, the three DEMA say there is a trend and say which way it goes.
Second, the RSI confirms that the strength is going in the same direction.
Only with both, the signal is eligible.
If one fails, there is no signal.
cenas.fala: Put the two parts together and you have the entry gate. First, the three DEMA say there is a trend and say which way it goes. Second, the RSI confirms that the strength is going in the same direction. Only with both, the signal is eligible. If one fails, there is no signal. That is not a preference, it is a closed door. And notice that this does not oblige you to pick the top or the bottom. It obliges you to wait for the market to show its hand before you show yours. Don't jump to conclusions from what you have just heard.

cenas.texto: DEMA aligned? · RSI confirming? · same direction?
cenas.fala: Do the exercise you will repeat in every lesson of this module. Choose a one-hour chart. First question: are the three averages ordered? Second: does the RSI confirm the same direction? Third: do both answers point to the same side? If the answer to any of them is "no", write "no signal" and move on to the next chart. It is not a failure. It is the filter doing its job, and doing it without asking you for an opinion. There is no shortcut here, and that is why it is worth practising. Write this in your notebook before you move on.

cenas.fala: When the price goes your way, the problem changes. It is no longer what you do if you are wrong. It is what you do when you are right.

cenas.titulo: The three targets sit at one and a half, three and six times the risk.
cenas.fala: The three targets sit at one and a half, three and six times the risk. They are not three predictions. They are three decision points. The first is the nearest, so it is the one reached first. The last is the most ambitious, and it may never be reached. A signal that reaches the second target did not fail at the first. Each target is a different moment, with its own decision, and that is why the plan separates them instead of lumping them into a single number. Don't jump to conclusions from what you have just heard.

cenas.texto: partial exit · written before entry
cenas.fala: Now the part that changes how you trade: partial exits. The idea is simple. You don't have to close the whole position in the same place. You can close one part at the first target, another at the second, and leave a part running for the third. What you have already collected stays collected, and what remains has room to run. But the percentage of each part is not a number you pick on top of the chart. It is a rule you write before entering. Decided during the trade, it is already emotion, and emotion tends to choose the wrong exit.

cenas.fala: Break-even is the step most people skip and later regret. When the price hits the first target, you can move the stop to the entry. If the market comes back, the part still open closes near zero, instead of giving back the full risk. Careful: this is your rule. Don't count on any button doing it for you, and the decision to apply it is entirely yours. Write it in the words you will use. For example: when the first target is hit, I close one part and move the stop to the entry.

Say you close one part and move the stop to one hundred. Then the market turns back and reaches one hundred. The part still open closes at break-even, and the part you collected at the first target stays as profit. If the price had dropped right after the entry, the loss would be the original stop, and nothing more. What the rule changes is what happens after the plan has proven it was right.
