cenas.titulo: Risk and position size
cenas.sub: 1% risk per trade · Calculating the size from the stop distance · Useful leverage and the account panel · Daily limit, losing streaks and stopping rules

cenas.titulo: 1% risk per trade
cenas.fala: You can have the best strategy in the world and still end up with no account. A run of big, bad trades is all it takes. The defence is not to be right more often. It is to lose a little at a time.

cenas.texto: This is the most tedious module of level three and, for many people, the most important.
cenas.aviso: Educational content. Not financial advice. The risk of loss is real.
cenas.fala: This is the most tedious module of level three and, for many people, the most important. Before we talk numbers, the usual warning. Educational content. The risk of loss is real, and it can be total. This lesson does not promise you will win. It promises you something more modest and more useful: that one bad trade will not take away what it took you years to build. That is the only promise a course on risk can honestly make. And even that depends on you, on following the rule every day, with no exceptions that seem reasonable at the time.

cenas.texto: 1% of the balance per trade
cenas.fala: The rule we are going to use is this: you risk at most one per cent of the balance on each trade. One per cent, not whatever you think the signal deserves. If you have €1,000 in your simulated account, the maximum risk of a trade is €10. And be careful: risk is not the amount invested. It is how much you lose if the stop is hit. They are different things, and confusing the two is the origin of many accounts that disappear. Notice that the gold slice is small on purpose. A small slice does not bring you down. Illustrative example, with a simulated account, as always.

cenas.titulo: invested €500 · stop −2% · risk €10

cartoes.d: Look at these two cases, illustrative examples.
In the first, you invest five hundred euros, but the stop is at two per cent.
If it is hit, you lose ten euros.

cenas.fala: Look at these two cases, illustrative examples. In the first, you invest five hundred euros, but the stop is at two per cent. If it is hit, you lose ten euros. In the second, you invest only two hundred, but the stop is at fifteen per cent, and you lose thirty. Anyone who only looks at the amount invested thinks the first is the big risk. They are wrong. The number that controls the account is the loss at the stop. So the right question is not "how much do I invest?", it is "how much do I lose if the stop is hit?". That question protects the balance, and it is the one we will train throughout the module.

cenas.texto: maximum risk = balance × 1%
cenas.fala: Write the formula at the top of your notebook: balance times one per cent. With a thousand simulated euros, the loss ceiling of each trade is ten euros. That ceiling does not change because the signal looks good to you. An exciting signal does not entitle you to risk more. A weak signal may lead you to risk less, and that is also fine. What changes from trade to trade is the size of the position, and that is next lesson. The risk stays fixed. If you ever write another number in your notebook, stop and go back to this page. The mistake is in the calculation, never in the market.

cenas.texto: ten losses in a row of 1% ≈ 10% of the account
cenas.fala: Let's be realistic. You will lose trades. That is part of the method and not a sign that the method is broken. With one per cent, a loss is a scratch. Ten losses in a row of one per cent each take roughly ten per cent off the account. It is a bad stretch, and it recovers with patience and rules. What destroys accounts is the opposite: risking ten or twenty per cent on one trade because this time is different. If you ever hear that sentence in your head, remember the formula. It does not argue. It calculates. And that is why it works.

cenas.texto: 1% of the balance · risk is the loss at the stop · €1,000 → €10
cenas.fala: Summary. The risk of each trade is one per cent of the balance. It is not what you invest, it is what you lose if the stop is hit. This rule protects you from streaks, because no single loss can take you out of the game. It also forces you to do something DCA has already taught you: decide the size before you feel the pressure of the market. In the next lesson we take this rule and calculate the exact size of the position, from the stop distance you learned in module twelve. It is not magic. It is a division.

cenas.texto: €10, one per cent. Illustrative example.
cenas.fala: You have €1,000 in a simulated account. What is the maximum risk on one trade? €10, one per cent. Illustrative example.

cenas.titulo: Calculating the size from the stop distance
cenas.fala: You already know how much you can lose: ten euros. The question almost nobody asks is still missing: how much can I buy so that, if the stop is hit, I lose exactly those ten?

cenas.titulo: Illustrative example, as always.
itens: The simulated account has a thousand euros and the maximum risk is ten.
It is not a number you guess.
It has a formula, and the formula fits on a card.
cenas.fala: Let's use the module twelve example, with the entry at one hundred and the stop two per cent below, at ninety-eight. Illustrative example, as always. The simulated account has a thousand euros and the maximum risk is ten. The question is: how much should I have invested in this position so that the stop, if hit, costs exactly ten euros? It is not a number you guess. It has a formula, and the formula fits on a card. I will show it to you slowly, with the calculator in hand, so that you can redo the calculation yourself without looking at me.
cenas.cap: Calculating the size from the stop distance
Calculating the size from the stop distance
cenas.texto: Size = risk in € ÷ stop distance in %
cenas.fala: The formula is this: the size of the position equals the risk in euros divided by the stop distance in percentage. The risk is ten euros. The stop distance is two per cent. Ten divided by two per cent, or by zero point zero two in the calculator, gives five hundred. Five hundred euros of position. If the price falls two per cent, you lose two per cent of five hundred, which is ten euros. Exactly your risk, not a cent more. Each piece has a role: the risk sets the ceiling, the stop sets the distance, and the size is what fits between the two.

cenas.titulo: stop 2% → position €500 · stop 4% → €250 · stop 5% → €200

cartoes.d: Notice what happens when you change only the stop distance, keeping the risk at ten euros.
With the stop at two per cent, the position is five hundred euros.
With the stop at four per cent, it drops to two hundred and fifty.

cenas.fala: Notice what happens when you change only the stop distance, keeping the risk at ten euros. With the stop at two per cent, the position is five hundred euros. With the stop at four per cent, it drops to two hundred and fifty. With the stop at five per cent, it is two hundred. The risk is always ten. A wider stop forces a smaller position. A tighter stop lets you buy more. Illustrative example, but the lesson is firm: never choose the size before you know where the stop is. The stop decides the position, not the other way round.
cenas.cap: Calculating the size from the stop distance
Calculating the size from the stop distance
cenas.texto: 1 balance · 2 risk of 1% · 3 stop distance in % · 4 size = 2 ÷ 3
cenas.fala: Write the procedure in four steps, always in the same order. One: the account balance. Two: the risk, one per cent of that balance. Three: the stop distance in percentage, taken from the signal plan. Four: you divide two by three. That result is the size. If you don't have the stop distance, you don't have a signal, and no size can be calculated. Don't guess the distance or round it to whatever suits you. It comes from the plan written before you entered, and that is where it should stay.

cenas.texto: €10 ÷ 3% = €333 → rounded down to €330
cenas.fala: Second example, also illustrative. The stop is now at three per cent. Ten divided by zero point zero three gives three hundred and thirty-three. You don't round up. Rounding up is increasing the risk without meaning to, and an account that grows without you noticing is exactly what we want to avoid. You round down, to three hundred and thirty, without hesitating. Notice that the wider stop gave a smaller position, as we saw a moment ago. The rule always adds up, and that is what makes it reliable. When it doesn't, the mistake is in the calculation.

cenas.texto: Stop first, size after.
cenas.fala: Summary. Stop first, size after. The formula is the risk in euros divided by the stop distance in percentage, and you always round down. There is no opinion in this calculation. There is a distance, a risk and a result. If one day you feel the size "should" be bigger because the signal is good, remember this lesson: conviction is not part of the formula. In the next lesson we look at leverage, which many people confuse with size, and at the Aurum Flow account panel, which shows several of these calculations already done.

cenas.titulo: Useful leverage and the account panel
cenas.fala: Leverage is the button most people confuse with position size. And confusing the two is the shortest route to losing more than you wanted.

cenas.titulo: leverage ≠ size ≠ risk
itens: Let's separate three things that look like one.
Size, or notional, is the total value of the position.
And risk is how much you lose if the stop is hit.
cenas.fala: Let's separate three things that look like one. Leverage is the multiplier the platform gives you to open a position bigger than the money you have deposited. Size, or notional, is the total value of the position. And risk is how much you lose if the stop is hit. Leverage does not create risk out of nothing. It changes how much money you have to set aside as margin, and it makes it easy to open large positions without noticing. If the size and the stop have not changed, the risk has not changed either, whatever leverage you chose.
cenas.cap: Useful leverage and the account panel
Useful leverage and the account panel
cenas.texto: useful leverage · notional · fees · risk % per trade
cenas.fala: The Aurum Flow account panel shows four things for the size you chose. The useful leverage: the leverage the position needs for the size you chose, not the maximum the platform offers. The notional, which is the total value of the position. The cost in fees, on entry and exit, which eats part of the result. And the risk as a percentage per trade. The values on screen are blurred, because they do not matter for the lesson. What matters is learning to read all four, not memorizing numbers.

cenas.texto: account €1,000 · position €500 · useful leverage ≈ 1×
cenas.fala: Apply this to the example from a moment ago: a thousand-euro account, a five-hundred-euro position. The useful leverage is low, about one times. That means the position fits in the account without stretching anything. Now imagine the panel showed you ten times for the same position. What would change? The size would still be five hundred, and the stop would still be at two per cent. The only thing that would change is the margin the platform asks to hold the position. Whoever chooses the leverage is not choosing the risk. The risk was already written into the stop and the formula.
cenas.cap: Useful leverage and the account panel
Useful leverage and the account panel
cenas.texto: use the leverage the size requires, never the maximum
cenas.fala: The rule you write in your notebook is this, without exceptions: the leverage I use is the one the calculated size requires, never the maximum offered, even if the platform presents it as the normal option. If the account fits without leverage, I don't use leverage. If the position needs some leverage, the panel shows it to you. And you always check the notional before you press confirm. It is not a rule of fear, it is a rule of precision. The platform shows the maximum because that is what it shows. Your interest is different: it is the size you calculated in the previous lesson, and nothing else.

cenas.texto: illustrative example: 0.1% fee per side · position €500 → €0.50 on entry + €0.50 on exit
cenas.fala: Finally, fees. In an illustrative example, with a fee of zero point one per cent per side, a five-hundred-euro position pays fifty cents on entry and fifty cents on exit. It seems little. But with a two per cent stop and a risk of ten euros, one euro of fees is ten per cent of the risk you defined. It is not a detail. That is why the panel shows the cost, and why you look at it before you confirm, not after. The real fee is your platform's, and it is in its terms. Check it. Don't use mine as if it were yours.

cenas.fala: Summary. Leverage is how the platform asks for margin. Size is the value of the position. Risk is the loss at the stop. Don't confuse the three. The Aurum Flow panel shows the useful leverage, the notional, the fees and the risk per trade, and your rule is to look at all four before pressing any button. In the last lesson of the module we talk about what happens after a loss, after a bad day, and how to stop in time, before a bad day turns into a bad week.

cenas.titulo: Daily limit, losing streaks and stopping rules
cenas.fala: The worst decision in an account is rarely the first loss. It is the fourth, after a bad morning, when you decide that 'now is the time'.

cenas.texto: a bad day can also be planned for
cenas.fala: Last lesson of the module, and perhaps the one that saves you the most. Everything we have seen so far is about single trades. But whoever loses money almost always loses in sequence. One loss, then another, then a third, and the head starts asking for an immediate recovery. That urge has a name: chasing losses. And the antidote is not willpower, which runs out quickly. It is a rule written before the day starts. Whoever decides what to do after three losses at ten in the morning is already deciding with a head in revenge mode. That is why the decision has to be made beforehand.

cenas.titulo: Look at this series, illustrative example.
cenas.fala: Look at this series, illustrative example. Three losses of one per cent each. On the thousand-euro account, that is around thirty euros. It hurts, but it is not the end. The problem starts when the fourth trade comes out bigger, because the person wants to recover quickly. At that moment, the risk stops being the one per cent of the rule and becomes a desperate bet. Nobody decides that on purpose. It happens gradually, with the justification that "this time it pays off". The stopping rule exists to prevent that shift, and so you don't have to argue about it with yourself in the worst moment.
cenas.cap: Daily limit, losing streaks and stopping rules

cenas.texto: daily limit · losing streak · stop is stop
cenas.fala: Write three stopping rules, with your own numbers. The first is the daily loss limit. For example, and it is only an illustrative example, two per cent of the balance in one day: once you hit it, you close the platform. The second is the losing streak: three losses in a row on the same day, and you stop. The third is the most important: after a stop, you don't come back to the screen that day, not even to "see if the signal has improved". This is the rule that saves the most accounts, because the market owes you nothing and it will always be back tomorrow. The numbers you write are yours. The ones I use here are small on purpose.

cenas.fala: Before each session, run a two-minute routine. Is the daily limit written down? Is the losing streak written down? Do you know the maximum number of trades you will take? Have you checked the news in the window? If the answer to any of these is no, you don't start. Notice that this routine says nothing about the market. It says everything about you. It is the part of trading that most resembles the Friday ritual of the DCA: rules before the money, not during it. Someone who has this routine done does not need to be smarter than the market. They need to be more predictable than their own emotions.

cenas.fala: If there is one thing the market teaches quickly, it is this: emotion does not wait until you are ready. So before any money, we train in a place where a mistake costs no real money.

cenas.texto: Before we start, a warning that applies to this whole module.
cenas.aviso: Educational content. Not financial advice. The risk of loss is real.
cenas.fala: Before we start, a warning that applies to this whole module. Educational content. The risk of loss is real. In this lesson you get to know the tools you will practise with, and the first rule is the most important of all: practice is done in a simulated account, never with rent money, never with money you need for the month's bills. I know it is tempting to skip this part and go straight to the real account. Don't skip it. Those who train calmly learn what haste hides. We will look at the three pieces of this module: the MTM WebTrader, the MTM Funded simulated account and, further on, MTM Auto. None of this is a shortcut to making money. It is a place to learn to do things well, with written rules, before any real risk.

cenas.titulo: First piece: the MTM WebTrader.
cenas.fala: First piece: the MTM WebTrader. It is the browser version of the MoreThanMoney execution tool. You open it on the computer, you see the asset's chart and the panel where orders are placed. You don't need to know everything at once. At this stage, what matters is one thing only: understanding where each element of the screen is before you touch any button. Whoever clicks without knowing where they are is not training, they are improvising. And improvising with emotion, on a screen with buy and sell buttons, is the simplest recipe for a decision you will regret.

cenas.titulo: MTM Funded simulated account
itens: Second piece: the MTM Funded simulated accounts.
Notice the word on the screen: simulated.

cenas.fala: Second piece: the MTM Funded simulated accounts. Notice the word on the screen: simulated. These are simulation accounts, with money that does not exist. There is no real deposit, no withdrawal, no real balance to lose. What you train here is the method: the entry, the stop, the size, the record. When emotion appears, and it will, the difference is this: the money is simulated, but the discipline you practise is real. Be careful, though. A simulated account does not reproduce the nerves of losing real money. So the test of the simulation is not winning. It is following the rules, trade by trade, even when the account looks small and the temptation looks big.

MTM WebTrader and the MTM Funded simulated account
cenas.texto: 1 · open the simulated account · 2 · choose one asset from your plan · 3 · write the rule before clicking
cenas.fala: How you train, in practice. First, you open the simulated account in the WebTrader. Second, you choose a single asset, one you already know from the earlier modules. Third, and this is the step people skip: you write the rule before clicking. Why you enter, where the stop goes, what the size is, and what you will do if the price moves against you. Only then do you place the order. If you can't write the rule in two sentences, you don't enter. This sounds like bureaucracy, and it is. Bureaucracy is what protects you from emotion at the moment it appears with the most force, which is almost always when the price moves fast.

cenas.texto: Simulation trains the method. It proves nothing.
cenas.fala: One last note, because it is easy to fool yourself. A simulated account that goes up does not prove the strategy works. A simulated account that goes down does not prove you are bad. What the simulation shows is whether you followed your own process, and that is the only indicator that matters to you at this stage. Don't look at the balance as a trophy. And if someone shows you a screenshot of a simulated account with a high balance, as proof that they make money, be suspicious. A screenshot is not a statistic, and a training account is not a real track record. When you need a number, ask for the full series of trades, not the pretty picture. Illustrative example, of course: a screenshot with a high balance can hide a hundred trades without a single written rule.

cenas.fala: Copying looks like the solution for those who don't have time. But there is one question almost nobody asks before switching it on: who answers for what happens afterwards?

cenas.fala: Third piece of this module: MTM Auto. It is MoreThanMoney's tool for copying strategies, and the keyword is this: with rules and limits. In other words, it is not a button that copies everything blindly. Before you switch on a strategy, you have to see which rules it follows and which limits the tool applies. This is very different from copying someone who turned up in a message group, without knowing anything about what that person does. Here there are rules in plain view, and that is already half the way to an informed decision. But only half. The other half is yours.

cenas.titulo: Before you switch on any strategy, read three things.
itens: First, what it does: which markets it works in, with what kind of entries and how often.
Second, the limits that apply on your side of the copy.

cenas.fala: Before you switch on any strategy, read three things. First, what it does: which markets it works in, with what kind of entries and how often. Second, the limits that apply on your side of the copy. Third, what happens when things go wrong. If you cannot say, in your own words, what the strategy does and what happens in the worst case, don't switch it on. And notice something that seems counterintuitive: a strategy that has been rising for a long time does not, for that reason, carry less risk. It may even carry more, because confidence grows just before a fall.
cenas.cap: MTM Auto: copying with rules and limits

cenas.texto: Copying is not delegating responsibility.
cenas.fala: Now the part that matters most. Copying does not take away your responsibility. When you switch on a copy, you remain the owner of the decision to have switched it on. The tool executes, but whoever chose the strategy, whoever decided how much they are willing to risk, and whoever decides to stop, is you. This holds even when the strategy belongs to someone you trust, and even when the tool is the house's own. The tool executes what is written. It does not know how much of your money is rent money, it does not know you have a bill to pay on Friday, and it does not know that you are tired and eager to win back a loss. Only you know those things, and only you can take them into account.

She was trying to win back a loss. The tool did exactly what was written. The mistake was not writing down her own limit. cenas.titulo: The trading journal
cenas.fala: If it isn't written down, it didn't happen. That sounds exaggerated, until we notice how many decisions we make from memory, and how often we recount them wrongly.

cenas.titulo: template in the course notebook
itens: This lesson is about the trading journal.
It is not a pretty dossier.
It is a page where you write each trade before, during and after.
cenas.fala: This lesson is about the trading journal. It is not a pretty dossier. It is a page where you write each trade before, during and after. The full template comes in the student notebook, but the idea is simple: a trade that is not in the journal, for learning purposes, did not exist. Because memory is generous with wins and cruel with mistakes. A week later, you remember having been right. You don't remember having entered outside the rule, or having moved the stop in a hurry. The journal exists to end that automatic selection our brain makes without asking permission.

cenas.texto: : date · asset · reason · rule · size · stop · targets. On the right,
cenas.fala: Let's go through the fields. Before entering, you record the date, the asset and the reason for the entry, written in one sentence, and which rule you are applying. You record the size of the position and how much you lose if the stop is hit, always in euros, never only in percentage. And you record the stop and the targets. Before you touch the button, the journal already has everything. After closing, you add the result, whether the rule was followed, and one line about what you felt. Illustrative example: "I entered because the price returned to the average; I lose twenty euros if the stop is hit; I followed the rule; I felt rushed at ten in the morning.

cenas.texto: rule followed? yes or no
cenas.fala: The most important column is the one almost nobody fills in: was the rule followed, yes or no. Because the goal at this stage is not to win. It is to execute the process you wrote. A losing trade with the rule followed is a good training trade. A winning trade outside the rule is a warning, not a compliment. If you mark "no" and the trade made a profit, write exactly that, without excuses. That "no" will be the most useful piece of information you get in a whole week, because it shows you where emotion got involved, even when it went well. Always write it, even when the answer bothers you.

cenas.titulo: Illustrative case: Rui, twenty-nine, made three trades in one week.
itens: On the first, he followed the rule and lost the expected amount, without drama.
When he did the review, the last two lines had "no" in the rule column.
That was when he understood the problem.
cenas.fala: Illustrative case: Rui, twenty-nine, made three trades in one week. On the first, he followed the rule and lost the expected amount, without drama. On the second, he moved the stop halfway through, because he didn't want to watch the loss grow. On the third, he entered with no written reason, just because the chart seemed to be moving fast. When he did the review, the last two lines had "no" in the rule column. That was when he understood the problem. It was not the market. It was him stepping out of the process, twice, in silence. The journal showed that in two minutes. Memory would have hidden it all.

cenas.texto: Write before. Close after. Never rewrite.
cenas.fala: Two rules so you don't spoil the journal. First: write before you enter. A journal written afterwards is a story, and stories adjust themselves. Second: never rewrite an old line. If you get a word wrong, you cross it out and write over it, with the date of the correction. If you erase what you did badly, you are erasing the only thing that can teach you. The journal is not there to judge you. It is there to show yourself what you really did, dated today and without makeup. Take this out of the notebook and keep it in view, so you can reread it before each session.

cenas.titulo: Weekly audit and the 30-minute routine
cenas.fala: Thirty minutes a week, with the journal open in front of you. Without this routine, the journal is just a notebook full of lines.

cenas.titulo: prepare 5 · review trades 10 · audit rules 10 · decide 5
itens: This is the routine.
Thirty minutes, once a week, always on the same day and at the same time.
Thirty minutes is short on purpose.
cenas.fala: This is the routine. Thirty minutes, once a week, always on the same day and at the same time. It breaks down like this: five minutes to prepare, ten to review the week's trades, ten to audit the rules, and five to decide on one single thing to change. Notice the time. Thirty minutes is short on purpose. A review that lasts three hours turns into anxiety, and a five-minute review turns into an excuse. Thirty minutes is enough to be honest, and not so long that you want to change everything at once. Choose the day and time in your calendar, as if it were a booked meeting.

cenas.titulo: First, review the trades.
itens: Don't look at the result in euros as a judge.
The result is a data point, and a single data point deceives.
A week of profit with three rules broken is a bad week.
cenas.fala: First, review the trades. You open the week's journal and read each line from top to bottom, without editing anything. You look for three things: how many trades you made, how many followed the rule, and at what moments you stepped out of the process. Don't look at the result in euros as a judge. The result is a data point, and a single data point deceives. A week of profit with three rules broken is a bad week. A week of loss with all rules followed is a well-trained week. Read with a pencil in hand and mark the lines that make you uncomfortable, without correcting them.

cenas.titulo: audit · size within the plan? · stop moved? · entry with no written reason? · rule by rule, with proof from the journal
itens: Was the size within what you defined?
Was the stop moved?
Was there any entry with no written reason?
cenas.fala: Then, the audit. For each rule written in your plan, you answer yes or no, with evidence taken from the journal. Was the size within what you defined? Was the stop moved? Was there any entry with no written reason? Any "no" is a point of attention, and every point of attention has a cause. The most frequent cause is almost never technical. It is emotional: boredom, haste, the urge to recover, fear of missing the rise. Give it a name, write it beside the line, and see whether it repeats the following week. It is not a punishment. It is a cool-headed reading, done with the same calm you would bring to reviewing any other process.

cenas.texto: One thing to change this week.
cenas.fala: Now, the hardest step: deciding one thing. Only one. Ask yourself which mistake repeated the most, and write a concrete rule to avoid it. For example: from now on, no order goes in without a written reason. And here is the golden rule of this lesson: don't change the rules halfway through the week. Change them on review day, after you have seen them written down. Changing everything on the back of the last trade is the quickest way to never know what works and what doesn't. If the change is too big, shrink it until it fits in a single sentence.

cenas.titulo: fixed day and time · journal open · audit · one change · review log
itens: Last step, and this one is not to be skipped: log the review itself.
Date, number of trades, number of rules followed, and the change you chose.
And if one week you can't, do the short version: ten minutes, just the audit.
cenas.fala: Last step, and this one is not to be skipped: log the review itself. Date, number of trades, number of rules followed, and the change you chose. That way, three months from now, you can see whether your discipline went up or down, and not just what you feel about it. Thirty minutes a week, without fail, is worth more than a study marathon that never repeats. And if one week you can't, do the short version: ten minutes, just the audit. Something small and done beats something big and postponed. Without a log, the review did not happen.

cenas.titulo: Stopping rules, psychology and the level 3 mission
cenas.fala: The worst decision of a market day is almost never the first. It is the fourth, made to win back the third.

cenas.titulo: in large letters and, below, three items:
itens: These are the rules that say when you stop, before you start arguing with yourself.
Write them with the numbers you choose.
There is no magic number, not even mine.
cenas.fala: We have reached the last lesson of the module, and the part that decides whether the others are worth anything. Stopping rules. These are the rules that say when you stop, before you start arguing with yourself. There can be three: a maximum number of consecutive losses, a maximum loss amount for the day, and a time after which you do not enter. Write them with the numbers you choose. There is no magic number, not even mine. There is your number, written beforehand and kept. And if the number is hit, the day ends there, even if the chart is doing exactly what you wanted.
cenas.cap: Stopping rules, psychology and the level 3 mission
Stopping rules, psychology and the level 3 mission
cenas.texto: I increase the size
cenas.fala: Now psychology, without beating around the bush. There is a classic spiral. You lose a trade and feel the urge to win it back. You increase the size of the next one, to recover faster. You lose again, because the bigger position amplifies the loss, and you enter a third to plug the hole. Each step seems reasonable at the time. Together they are a disaster. Break this spiral with a simple rule: never increase the size after a loss. The size is the one in the plan, always, the one you wrote before any emotion showed up. Notice that the spiral does not need greed. The urge to plug a hole is enough.

cenas.titulo: And when you feel emotion taking over, use the pause.
itens: The pause is not weakness.
Close the conversation, breathe, and go back to your plan.
cenas.fala: And when you feel emotion taking over, use the pause. If you have hit a stopping rule, or if you feel you can't think clearly, close the WebTrader and don't come back that day. If you really want to look at a market again, wait twenty-four hours and come back with the journal in front of you. The pause is not weakness. It is the cheapest rule there is, and the one that saves the most money for whoever uses it. If someone tells you that you have to decide now, because the opportunity won't come back, you already know what that is. Close the conversation, breathe, and go back to your plan.

cenas.fala: Illustrative case: Tiago, forty, had no stopping rule. One morning, he lost two trades in a row and decided he would recover before lunch. It was not the first time he had thought that way, but it was the first time the journal was in front of him. He wrote, without meaning to: "I want to win it back". That sentence gave everything away. He closed the screen. At the Friday review, he realised the losses that morning had the same origin: haste. Illustrative example, of course, because what matters is the pattern, not the value of each trade. Think about this during your next week, before you need it.

cenas.fala: With crypto, tax is not paid on the day you buy. It can show up, however, on the day you sell, if you are not prepared.

cenas.kicker: 28% on the gain, not on the total
cenas.titulo: That said, there is a basic principle you should know.

The purchase date and the sale date count days, and a single day's difference can change everything.
